question: A test catches 90% of cases and wrongly flags 9% of healthy people. Someone tests positive. How likely is it real?
answer: It depends on who was tested, and counting people shows how. Of 1,000 screened with 10 ill, 9 test positive truly and 89 falsely: a positive is real about one time in 11. In a 1998 study of 48 doctors, correct answers rose from about 10% with probabilities to 46% with such counts.
move: Turn percentages into counts of people, and hard problems become easy.
ask: Next time a percentage confuses me, could I picture 1,000 people and count what happens to them?
reference: Hoffrage & Gigerenzer, Using natural frequencies to improve diagnostic inferences, Academic Medicine, 1998; Gigerenzer et al., Helping Doctors and Patients Make Sense of Health Statistics, Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 2007

notes.text: 1 ill in 1,000: about 1 true positive among 91. Almost every positive is wrong.
10 in 1,000, a typical screening: 9 real positives, 89 false. About 1 in 11.
100 in 1,000, a group with symptoms, say: now half the positives are real.
300 in 1,000: four in five. Same test, different people.
